In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a new dendroclimatology-based archive of large volcanic eruption events over the past thousand years.
the development of a new proxy archive for the last millennium and its application to evaluate climate sensitivity estimates to volcanic forcing.
the development of a novel approach to identify volcanic events and to estimate the associated cooling magnitude in the last millennium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the climate response to large volcanic eruptions during the past millennium is likely to have been between 0.4 °C and 1.0 °C, with a best estimate of 0.6 °C.
the volcanic impact on Northern Hemisphere climate during the past millennium has been substantial, but the exact magnitude of the cooling is difficult to estimate.
the volcanic impact on Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures is in the range of 0.5–1.0 °C.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our method provides a robust tool to identify and date volcanic eruptions in the past millennium, and it is an independent benchmark of the forcing estimates from ice cores.
the volcanic forcing of climate is well captured by the new method and the dendroclimatological reconstructions.
the new method of break point detection applied to maximum latewood density records provides a robust and reliable archive of large volcanic eruption activity over the past millennium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the new dendroclimatically derived archive of volcanic activity is an independent and valuable addition to the existing volcanic forcing records.
the new method of break point analysis in tree rings provides a valuable tool for identifying large volcanic eruptions and their climatic impact in the last millennium.
the new method can be applied to a wide variety of temperature proxies to detect large volcanic eruptions and their climatic impact.
